blocks.title: Isomerism
blocks.text: Two or more compounds having the same molecular formula but different structural formulas and properties are isomers, and the phenomenon is isomerism. The structural formula shows the arrangement of atoms and bonds in the compound.

The simplest hydrocarbon with structural isomers is butane, C4H10: in butane and higher alkanes the atoms can be arranged in more than one way that satisfies all valencies, so two or more different arrangements share one molecular formula. Chlorobutane has two arrangements, CH3CH2CH2CH2Cl (1-chlorobutane) and CH3CHClCH2CH3 (2-chlorobutane), and experiment confirms two compounds with different physical properties and the same formula C4H9Cl. Isomerism is common once a compound has more than three carbon atoms, and the number of possible isomers increases very rapidly with the number of carbons: pentane has three isomers.

blocks.prompt: Why has methane, ethane or propane no structural isomer, while butane has?
blocks.explanation: With one, two or three carbons there is only one way to join the carbons in a chain, so only one structure satisfies the valencies. With four carbons the fourth can be joined to the end of a three-carbon chain (butane) or to its middle carbon (2-methylpropane), giving two different compounds with the formula C4H10.

items: Isomers: same molecular formula, different structural formula and properties; first in butane C4H10; C4H9Cl has 1- and 2-chlorobutane; pentane has three isomers; the count rises fast with carbon number.
